q: What is the largest n at which a *full-register* bucket-brigade qRAM circuit (every trit qubit pair instantiated, every routing gate compiled to a Clifford+T Toffoli net) can be simulated end-to-end on a single workstation, and how does the circuit-depth picture (as opposed to just active-switch count) evolve with the fan-in/fan-out of the per-level trit-update Toffoli net?
basis: In this replication only n=2 was simulated with the full 9-qubit register (addr+trits+bus); n=3 and n=4 relied on a reduced (addr,bus) subspace equivalence because dim = 2^(n + 2*(2^n-1) + 1) blows up (~2^35 already at n=4). A direct full-register benchmark up to n=6 or so would empirically validate the claim in a way an analytical reduction cannot, and would surface the depth cost hidden by the abstract active-switch counting.
next_steps: Compile the trit-update per level as an explicit CNOT/Toffoli net in Qiskit, run Aer statevector for n=3,4,5,6 with time and RAM logs, and record (a) simulated wall time, (b) two-qubit gate count, (c) circuit depth, alongside the abstract active-switch count.

q: Under a realistic single-qubit depolarizing + dephasing noise model on the trit qubits, at what per-trit error rate does the bucket-brigade advantage over conventional fanout actually invert — i.e. is there a small-N regime where BB loses because its per-call routing sequence is deeper even though it excites fewer switches?
basis: Every fidelity we measured is 1.0 because the simulator is noiseless. The paper's error-resilience claim is asymptotic and the crossover point vs conventional fanout is not drawn explicitly; a noisy Aer run for small N would map the crossover empirically and validate (or bound) the paper's headline decoherence-advantage claim.
next_steps: Add Aer NoiseModel with p ranging log-scale over [1e-4, 1e-1] on trits and address qubits, run both BB and fanout implementations for N in {4,8,16}, and plot query fidelity vs p for both.

q: How does the BB protocol degrade under imperfect trit reset — if a small residual amplitude in |left>/|right> persists on some non-carved trits after a call, how does the leakage into the 'out-of-protocol' subspace compound over M successive queries, and does that leakage grow faster than address-register error?
basis: The replication's reduced-subspace simulation is only valid on the WAIT-initialised protocol subspace; it treats non-WAIT initial trits as identity. The paper implicitly assumes perfect uncomputation of trits back to |WAIT>. Multi-call leakage is not analysed anywhere in the paper and is a natural robustness question for any real hardware realisation.
next_steps: Introduce a controlled leakage parameter epsilon per trit reset in the full-register simulator, iterate M calls of BB qRAM, and measure the ideal-state fidelity vs M and epsilon; compare against a simple address-line dephasing baseline.

q: The scaling table used 1-bit classical data (D_j in {0,1}). Eq. (1) of the paper is written for arbitrary quantum |D_j> registers. What are the exact additional switch, circuit-depth, and register-size costs when D_j itself is a k-qubit *quantum* register, and does the O(log N) active-switch scaling survive verbatim or become O(k log N)?
basis: The paper leaves the memory-array data type open ('classical or quantum'), and our reproduction uses the simplest classical-bit case. Extending to k-qubit quantum data is straightforward in principle but changes both the cost model (bus becomes a k-qubit register, bus-memory correlation becomes k CNOTs per call) and the entanglement footprint the paper's decoherence argument relies on.
next_steps: Generalise BucketBrigadeQRAM to k-qubit memory cells, re-derive the switch and depth counts for k = 1, 2, 4, 8, and check whether the O(log N) headline is preserved or acquires a k factor in the depth.

q: Is there a strictly smaller qubit encoding of the trit wait/left/right levels than the standard 2-qubits-per-trit qutrit-in-qubit embedding (which doubles the tree qubit count to 2*(2^n - 1)) that still preserves the BB active-switch advantage — e.g. a single-qubit amplitude marker or a shared-ancilla design — and if so what is the amplitude-encoding overhead trade-off versus the leaked-error overhead of the 2-qubit encoding?
basis: We used the standard qutrit-in-qubit embedding (|WAIT>=|00>, |left>=|01>, |right>=|10>) because it matches Hann 2021 / Di Matteo 2020, but the encoding overhead directly inflates the memory-tree qubit count by 2x versus the O(N) figure the paper counts in trit *nodes*. Whether a tighter encoding survives is not addressed in the original paper.
next_steps: Explore a 1-qubit-per-trit design with graded amplitude (e.g. |WAIT> ~ |0>, |left> ~ e^{i phi_L}|1>, |right> ~ e^{i phi_R}|1>) or an ancilla-shared design; check whether BB routing remains a well-defined permutation on the protocol subspace and quantify leakage-into-invalid-states rate.
